---
title: "Bayesian"
---

Every method so far has answered "how high is too high" by looking up comparable
weeks and asking how far above them this week sits. This one answers it
differently. It writes down a full probability distribution for what next week's
count could be, then cuts that distribution at a high quantile and calls
everything above the cut a signal.

The difference lives entirely in the tail. A distribution built from parameters
you pretend to know is narrower than one built from parameters you admit you had
to estimate, and a narrower distribution puts the threshold lower than it should
be. Raise the uncertainty slider below and watch the two thresholds come apart.

::: {#fig-predictive}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-predictive"></div>
```

Two predictive distributions for the same week. The grey outline fixes the
parameters at their estimates; the blue one averages over what they might be. The
shaded band is the gap between the thresholds they produce.
:::

The algorithm is BODA, the Bayesian Outbreak Detection Algorithm of Manitz and
Höhle [@manitz2013], implemented in R's `surveillance` package as `boda()`
[@salmon2016]. Salmon and colleagues later extended it to handle reporting delay
[@salmon2015], which is `bodaDelay()`.

## What a reference set leaves behind {#sec-bayes-limits}

Before the method, the complaint it answers. Reference-value methods — the CUSUM
and RKI chapters both belong here — pay for their simplicity in four ways.

::: {.algo-step}
**They use a sliver of the data.** A handful of weeks from a handful of years
decides the threshold. The rest of the series still carries information about
trend and seasonality, and none of it is read.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**The answer depends on a window you chose.** How many years back, how many weeks
either side. @sec-rki-size showed those choices fixing the size of the comparison
before any data is read, and nothing in the method tells you which choice is right.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**They act as though the estimate were the truth.** The reference mean is
substituted straight into the predictive distribution, as if it were known rather
than estimated. This is the plug-in step, and it is what narrows the distribution
and drops the threshold.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**There is nowhere to put a cause.** Cases rise for reasons — weather, population
movement, a change in who gets tested. A reference set has no slot for any of them.
:::

One clarification is worth making before going further, because the chapter title
invites the wrong reading. The line that separates these two families is not
frequentist against Bayesian. It is **reference values against a regression
model**. The Bayesian framework by itself fixes only the third complaint, the
plug-in step. The other three fall only because the method moves to a full
regression on the whole series.

The package makes the point for you. `surveillance` also ships `algo.bayes`, which
is Bayesian and still reference-value based — and still has all three of the other
problems.

## Computing an epidemic threshold with BODA {#sec-bayes-threshold}

`boda()` runs in six steps. The first three build a model, the fourth fits it, and
the last two turn the fit into a number you can compare a count against.

::: {.algo-step}
**1. Choose the distribution.** Case counts almost always vary more than their own
mean, because transmission clusters and so the observations are not independent.
@sec-rki-dispersion made that case in full; BODA takes it as the starting point and
uses a negative binomial throughout:

$$ y_t \mid \mu_t, \nu \;\sim\; \mathrm{NB}(\mu_t, \nu), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(y_t) = \mu_t + \frac{\mu_t^2}{\nu}. $$

Watch the direction of $\nu$, which is easy to read backwards. A **larger** $\nu$
means **less** spread; as $\nu \to \infty$ the distribution collapses to Poisson.
It measures the inverse of overdispersion.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**2. Model the expected count.** Everything that should move the expectation goes
into a linear predictor on the log scale:

$$ \log \mu_t \;=\; \log P_t + \alpha_{0t} + \beta t + \gamma_t + X_t^{\!\top}\delta + \zeta z_t. $$

Each term has one job. $\log P_t$ is a population offset, so the model works on
rates rather than raw counts and districts of different sizes can be compared.
$\alpha_{0t}$ is an intercept free to drift, smoothing the baseline level. $\beta t$
is long-run trend. $\gamma_t$ is the seasonal cycle, period 52 for weekly data.
$X_t^{\!\top}\delta$ is where covariates enter — temperature, absolute humidity,
rainfall, usually lagged. And $\zeta z_t$ marks weeks already flagged as
aberrant, so that old epidemic peaks are not learned as ordinary baseline.
:::

That last term deserves a second look, because it sounds like the objection raised
against reference methods: doesn't somebody have to decide in advance which weeks
were epidemic? No. In the implementation `z_t` is not supplied by the user. With
`pastAberrations = TRUE`, it is read from the alarms the algorithm itself raised at
earlier time points. The loop closes on its own.

::: {.algo-step}
**3. Put a prior on everything.** In a Bayesian model every parameter is a random
variable and needs a distribution before the data arrives. This model is a **latent
Gaussian model**, which splits the parameters into two tiers: a latent field
$x = (\alpha_{0t}, \beta, \gamma_t, \delta, \zeta)$ of regression coefficients and
random effects, assumed jointly Gaussian; and a small set of hyperparameters
$\theta = (\nu, \tau)$ controlling dispersion and how smooth each effect is.

The split is not bookkeeping. Keeping the hyperparameters few — under about
fifteen — is the condition that makes step 4 possible [@rue2009].
:::

In practice: the drifting intercept is declared through `f(time, model = ...)`,
where `rw1` (a first-order random walk, a slowly wandering baseline) is a sensible
default for weekly data, with `iid` and `rw2` as the looser and smoother
alternatives. Setting `season = TRUE` gives the seasonal term a cyclic spline, so
the end of one year joins the start of the next. Fixed coefficients get vague
Gaussian priors and let the data speak. For the hyperparameters INLA defaults to
log-Gamma; on short series or thin ward-level counts, a PC prior is less sensitive
to how you set it. Run the whole thing under at least two prior choices and check
the answer does not move.

::: {.algo-step}
**4. Fit it.** With weeks $1$ to $T-1$ in hand, Bayes' theorem gives

$$ p(x, \theta \mid y_{1:T-1}) \;\propto\; p(y_{1:T-1} \mid x, \theta)\, p(x \mid \theta)\, p(\theta). $$

The normalising constant is an integral with no closed form. MCMC would sample it
accurately and take hours for one series — impossible for a system that runs weekly
across hundreds of units. BODA uses INLA instead [@rue2009], a deterministic
approximation built for exactly this class of model, which matches MCMC closely and
runs orders of magnitude faster.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**5. Average over what you do not know.** The parameters were never the point. What
is wanted is $y_T$, and the distribution for it integrates the model away:

$$ p(y_T \mid y_{1:T-1}) \;=\; \int p(y_T \mid x, \theta)\, p(x, \theta \mid y_{1:T-1})\, \mathrm{d}x\, \mathrm{d}\theta. $$

This single line is the whole argument of the chapter. It folds together two
different uncertainties: counts bounce around even when the parameters are known
exactly, **and** the parameters are not known exactly. Plug-in methods carry only
the first.
:::

One implementation detail follows directly from step 4 and is easy to get wrong.
INLA returns the **marginal** posterior of each parameter, not their joint
distribution. `boda()` therefore takes a `samplingMethod` argument, and it should be
set to `'joint'`. Sampling each marginal independently discards the correlations
between parameters and narrows the predictive distribution — reintroducing, by the
back door, the exact defect the method exists to remove.

::: {.algo-step}
**6. Cut the tail.** The threshold is the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of that predictive
distribution. Counts are whole numbers, so the honest definition is the smallest
integer whose cumulative probability reaches $1-\alpha$:

$$ \xi_{1-\alpha} \;=\; \min\Bigl\{ k \in \{0,1,2,\dots\} \;:\; \textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{k} p(y_T = j \mid y_{1:T-1}) \;\ge\; 1-\alpha \Bigr\}. $$

A week signals when $y_T^{\text{obs}} > \xi_{1-\alpha}$.
:::

### Why the Bayesian threshold sits higher {#sec-bayes-variance}

The claim that the predictive distribution is wider can be made exact. Split its
variance by conditioning on the parameters first:

$$ \operatorname{Var}(y_T \mid \text{data}) \;=\; \operatorname{E}\!\bigl[\operatorname{Var}(y_T \mid \mu)\bigr] \;+\; \operatorname{Var}\!\bigl(\operatorname{E}[y_T \mid \mu]\bigr). $$

The first term is how much the counts would scatter if you knew where they were
centred. The second is how much the centre itself could move.

Substitute the negative binomial, for which $\operatorname{Var}(y \mid \mu) = \mu +
\mu^2/\nu$ and $\operatorname{E}[y \mid \mu] = \mu$:

$$ \operatorname{Var}(y_T \mid \text{data}) \;=\; \operatorname{E}[\mu] + \frac{\operatorname{E}[\mu^2]}{\nu} + \operatorname{Var}(\mu). $$

Write $\hat\mu = \operatorname{E}[\mu]$ and $s^2 = \operatorname{Var}(\mu)$, and use
$\operatorname{E}[\mu^2] = \hat\mu^2 + s^2$:

$$ \operatorname{Var}(y_T \mid \text{data}) \;=\; \underbrace{\hat\mu + \frac{\hat\mu^2}{\nu}}_{\text{plug-in}} \;+\; s^2\Bigl(1 + \frac{1}{\nu}\Bigr). $$

The brace is exactly what a plug-in method computes. Everything after it is what a
plug-in method discards, and it has a shape worth reading. The penalty grows with
the **square** of how uncertain the expected count is, so it stays negligible until
the estimate is genuinely shaky and then grows fast. And it is **larger when $\nu$
is small**: the more overdispersed the counts already are, the more parameter
uncertainty piles on top.

@fig-predictive opens at $\hat\mu = 15$, $\nu = 6$ and 30% uncertainty. The
plug-in variance is 52.50, the formula adds about 24.7, and the total is 77.17. In
cases, the plug-in threshold is 28 and the Bayesian one is 32 — and a threshold of
28 that advertises a 5% false alarm rate delivers 7.6%.

## When this week's count is not yet this week's count {#sec-bayes-delay}

For ward-level surveillance this is not a refinement. It is the main problem.

A week's count is never finished when the week is. Cases have to present, be
tested, be confirmed and be entered, and all of that takes time. So at the moment
the algorithm runs, the current week is **under-reported** — while the threshold it
is compared against was calibrated on historical weeks that have long since filled
in. The comparison is between an incomplete number and a complete-number threshold,
and it fails in the worst possible direction: outbreaks are missed precisely when
detecting them matters most.

::: {#fig-delay}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-delay"></div>
```

The same forty weeks under two rules. Hollow outlines are the counts once every
case has arrived; solid bars are what is visible when the week is judged. Rings
mark exceedances the rule fails to see.
:::

Set the wait to zero and read the figure as reported: only about a third of each
week's cases exist yet, and all three genuine exceedances slip under the threshold.
Wait two weeks and all three are caught — but every alarm now arrives two weeks
after the week it describes, which for a vector-borne outbreak is most of the window
in which a response would have helped.

The second tab is the way out. If you know what share of a week's cases has usually
arrived by a given delay, you can scale the partial count back up and judge the week
immediately. That is what delay correction does, and at a wait of zero it recovers
all three.

Salmon and colleagues built this into the model rather than bolting it on
[@salmon2015]. The data are treated as a two-way table — week of onset against
reporting delay — with the lower right corner missing, and that table is modelled
with negative binomial regression. The implementation is `bodaDelay()`, and using it
means preparing a **reporting triangle** rather than a plain weekly series.

Worth knowing before you plan around it: `bodaDelay()` combines the Manitz–Höhle
algorithm with Noufaily's [@noufaily2013], and so it still takes reference-window
arguments `b` and `w`. The dependence on a chosen window, the second complaint in
@sec-bayes-limits, is therefore **not** fully removed. That is a deliberate trade of
theoretical tidiness for something that runs.

## Practical notes {#sec-bayes-practice}

**The software is experimental.** `boda()` says so in its own documentation. It
depends on INLA, which is not on CRAN and installs from its own repository:

```r
install.packages("INLA", repos = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable")
```

It is slow, because a Bayesian model is fitted at every time point. And results are
not reproducible under INLA's default parallelism; for a reproducible run, set
`INLA::inla.setOption(num.threads = "1:1")` before `set.seed()`.

**Many units at once is a different problem.** This is the easiest thing to overlook
when moving from one series to a whole city. Run the algorithm across $N$ units at
level $\alpha$ and, with no outbreak anywhere, the expected number of false alarms
per week is $N\alpha$. For 168 units at $\alpha = 0.05$ that is about **eight false
alarms every week** — enough to exhaust a response team's trust within a few months.
The options are to lower $\alpha$ and accept the loss of sensitivity, to control a
false discovery rate rather than each alarm separately, or to require a signal to
repeat across weeks or cluster in space before it triggers fieldwork. Whichever you
pick, write down why.

**Use the population offset.** When units differ greatly in size, $\log P_t$ has to
enter the model as an offset. Without it, dense wards carry permanently high
thresholds and sparse ones alarm constantly, and neither reflects real risk. Check
whether the version of `boda()` you are running accepts an offset, since its `X`
argument takes covariates as fixed effects only.

## Measuring whether it works {#sec-bayes-evaluation}

A detection algorithm is worth only what it can be shown to do. The minimum set:
**sensitivity** (the share of real outbreaks detected), **specificity** and the
false alarm rate, and **timeliness** — an algorithm that detects everything four
weeks late detects nothing useful. Because the output here is a whole distribution
rather than a yes-or-no verdict, add a **proper scoring rule**, which grades the
probability forecast itself.

Evaluate on both simulated data, where the true outbreaks are known by
construction, and on real historical series, which is how Manitz and Höhle assessed
BODA [@manitz2013]. Unkel and colleagues give a fuller comparison framework
[@unkel2012].
